meta.title: Who really said "Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or says it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Malcolm X really said it — in a New York speech on 7 January 1965. But the transcript reads "no matter who does it or who says it."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or says it'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Malcolm X, from his 7 January 1965 Militant Labor Forum speech in New York — though the circulating wording quietly drops a word.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–1965 · American Black nationalist leader and human-rights activist
answer.sourceLine: He said it in “Prospects for Freedom in 1965,” delivered at the Socialist Workers Party’s Militant Labor Forum in New York City on 7 January 1965 — his third appearance at that forum. Published transcripts read “Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or who says it”; the version that circulates online quietly drops the second “who.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 7 January 1965 — Militant Labor Forum, New York City
Malcolm X Speaks, ed. George Breitman (1965)
Clipped — transcripts read “or who says it”

source.excerpt: That’s wrong. Now, you’re not supposed to be so blind with patriotism that you can’t face reality. Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or who says it.
trail: The passage survives in a published transcript headnoted to the Socialist Workers Party’s Militant Labor Forum in New York City, 7 January 1965: “That’s wrong. Now, you’re not supposed to be so blind with patriotism that you can’t face reality. Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or who says it” — Workers’ Voice ↗.

Two further independent transcripts carry the identical wording in the identical paragraph about the Congo and South Vietnam — ICIT Digital Library ↗ and AClasses ↗, the latter opening with his own words: “It is an honor to me to come back to the Militant Labor Forum again this evening. It’s my third time here.”
Of the aggregators we checked, only WIST ↗ attaches a real citation, naming the speech, the date of 7 January 1965, New York, and the collection Malcolm X Speaks.

That collection — Malcolm X Speaks: Selected Speeches and Statements, edited by George Breitman — “came out in 1965 … from Merit Publishers, a Trotskyist imprint” ↗, as Ibram X. Kendi records. It is still in print from Pathfinder Press ↗, and also from Grove Press ↗, whose 2024 paperback carries a Kendi introduction.
source.excerptNote: The sentence closes a passage on what the United States “did in the Congo in 1964” and was doing in South Vietnam. It is an argument about foreign policy and patriotism, not a free-floating maxim.

source.rightsNote: The speech was delivered on 7 January 1965 and published that same year — decades after the 1931 cut-off for the United States public domain — so both the address and the collected text remain in copyright. Malcolm X Speaks is in print from two houses, Pathfinder Press and Grove Press, so approach whichever published the edition you are quoting. Short quotation for identification and comment, as here, is a different matter from reproducing the speech; for anything longer, clear it with the rights holders.

author.name: Malcolm X
author.heading: Who was Malcolm X?
author.metaLine: 1925–1965 · American Black nationalist leader and human-rights activist
author.bio: Born Malcolm Little in Omaha, Nebraska in 1925, he became the Nation of Islam’s most forceful national spokesman before leaving the group, embracing Sunni Islam, and founding his own organizations. In the last year of his life he recast the Black freedom struggle in the United States as an international human-rights question, and spoke repeatedly to the Socialist Workers Party’s Militant Labor Forum in New York — this speech was his third such appearance. He was assassinated in Manhattan on 21 February 1965, just over six weeks after delivering it.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody is putting these words in the wrong mouth — Malcolm X really said them. What travels badly is the wording and the source. Both of the biggest quote sites carrying this line get one or the other wrong.

items.why: Published transcripts read “Now, you’re not supposed to be so blind with patriotism that you can’t face reality. Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or who says it.” The circulating form contracts the first clause to “you’re not to be” and drops the second “who” — compare the transcript ↗.
Goodreads files the line under that title ↗ and names no speech and no date. The documented origin is the Militant Labor Forum address of 7 January 1965.
The Quotations Page carries it ↗ with nothing but “US black nationalist leader (1925-1965)” attached — no speech, no venue, no year. That is how a real sentence starts to look like a fabricated one.

The line does not appear on English Wikiquote’s Malcolm X page ↗ in any section — sourced, disputed or misattributed. Its absence there is not evidence against the quote; it simply means the speech transcript has to do the work. Simple English Wikiquote ↗ does list the clipped wording, but only under “Attributed quotes” and with no citation — one more copy travelling without a source.

misattribution.truthLine: He said it on 7 January 1965, at the Militant Labor Forum in New York, in a paragraph about the Congo and South Vietnam — read the whole speech ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is not a greeting-card maxim, and it was never meant to be portable. The sentence lands at the end of a blunt passage about United States conduct abroad — what America “did in the Congo in 1964,” which Malcolm X calls “criminal,” and the war in South Vietnam, where he says American soldiers were dying “for no reason at all.” The point of “wrong is wrong” is the clause that sets it up: you’re not supposed to be so blind with patriotism that you can’t face reality.

He was speaking to the Socialist Workers Party’s Militant Labor Forum in New York, an audience he had addressed twice before. He opened by joking that the press would report the evening as though it had taken place “in Peking or someplace else” — a man well aware that being right about American foreign policy in January 1965 was not going to be reported as patriotism. He was killed six weeks later.
detailsBody: The clipped form almost certainly spread by transcription drift on quote-aggregator sites rather than by any deliberate rewrite: “you’re not supposed to be” contracts to “you’re not to be,” and the repeated “who” in “who does it or who says it” reads as redundant on the page even though it is emphatic in speech.
The meaning survives intact, which is why this page rates the quote verified rather than disputed — but if you are quoting him in print, quote the transcript.

schema.claimReviewed: Malcolm X said “Wrong is wrong, no matter who does it or who says it” — popularly quoted in the clipped form “no matter who does it or says it” — in “Prospects for Freedom in 1965,” his 7 January 1965 speech to the Militant Labor Forum in New York City. The attribution is verified; no published transcript carries the clipped wording.
